intro: Richard Penrose Arnold can never keep a serious conversation serious for long. Elgar gives him a solemn tune in the basses, then lets the woodwinds break in with jokes.

sections.label: A · Arnold begins solemnly
sections.mNote: Cellos and basses carry the C-minor theme

sections.label: B · The woodwinds interrupt
sections.mNote: C major, with quick flute and oboe replies

sections.label: Link · On towards Ysobel
sections.mNote: A quiet string figure keeps the music moving

cues.title: A solemn beginning
cues.text: Cellos and double basses set out the theme in C minor, marked sostenuto. The violins wind around it on their lowest strings. Arnold begins his conversation with a properly serious face.
cues.evidence: Novello full score, p. 24, rehearsal 15: sostenuto lower strings, violin figuration marked sul G. Elgar connects the theme’s solemnity with Arnold’s conversation in his commentary on variation V: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enigma_Variations
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The poet’s son at the piano
cues.text: Arnold, son of the poet Matthew Arnold, teaches himself the piano. Elgar enjoys the way he gets round the difficult bits while still conveying the music’s feeling. His conversation has the same freedom: earnest talk keeps breaking into whimsical remarks.
cues.evidence: Elgar’s recollections of Arnold’s piano playing and conversation, quoted in John Pickard’s BBC programme note (2005): https://www.bbc.com/radio3/classical/elgar/notes/note_enigma.shtml

cues.title: The conversation carries on
cues.text: The wind chatter subsides. Small string figures continue over quiet timpani and low brass, leading straight into Isabel Fitton’s portrait, Ysobel. Elgar writes attacca at the end of the page.
cues.evidence: Novello full score, pp. 29–30: chromatic closing link, soft trombones and tuba, timpani roll and attacca into variation VI.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The flute cracks a joke
transitions.how: The C-minor bass melody settles on C, and E♮ brightens the harmony into C major. A solo flute runs upwards while oboes and clarinets exchange short replies. The strings fall to pianissimo; the Moderato pace holds, though the conversation has become much less solemn.
transitions.evidence: Novello full score, p. 25, rehearsal 16: C in the bass, E naturals in the flute line, pianissimo strings and wind exchanges.

transitions.title: Low brass under the farewell
transitions.how: A falling clarinet run leads into the closing link. The strings keep a small curling figure moving while timpani hold a quiet roll. Trombones and tuba enter pianissimo, and the double basses sustain their note beneath them. The page ends attacca, carrying Arnold’s last sentence into Ysobel.
transitions.evidence: Novello full score, pp. 29–30: descending solo clarinet, sustained bass and timpani, pianissimo trombones and tuba, and the attacca marking.

source.title: Elgar, Enigma Variations, full score (Novello)
source.locator: Novello full score, pp. 24–30, rehearsal figures 15–18: the solemn C-minor melody, its C-major wind interruptions and the link into Ysobel.

timeline.note: Cellos and basses carry the solemn melody, with bassoon and horn replies (p. 24).
Short wind phrases interrupt in C major over quiet strings (pp. 25–26).
Wind and brass join the long melody while the strings keep moving beneath it (pp. 26–28).
The brass withdraw and short clarinet and flute replies return (pp. 28–29).
A clarinet run and moving strings lead into quiet low-brass chords and timpani (pp. 29–30).

composer.epithet: He made the Enigma Variations from his friendships and preserved his own way with the music on gramophone records.
facts: His father’s Worcester music shop; violin and organ; composition largely self-taught
Powick bandmaster, instrumental teacher and organist at St George’s, Worcester
Two symphonies; violin and cello concertos; Gerontius; five Pomp and Circumstance marches
Master of the King’s Musick from 1924; recordings of his own orchestral works
composer.background:
Elgar grew up among the instruments and sheet music in his father’s Worcester shop. William tuned pianos and played the organ at St George’s Catholic Church; Edward studied the scores, learned several instruments and earned money with his violin. Born at Lower Broadheath on 2 June 1857, he had hoped to study at Leipzig, but the family could not afford it. His education continued in rehearsal rooms. Playing in the Three Choirs Festival orchestra, he learned the choral music of Handel and Mendelssohn from inside the string section.

From 1879 to 1884 he was bandmaster at Worcester County Asylum, Powick. He trained members of staff to play for the patients and supplied quadrilles and polkas for the Friday-evening dances. Here was an orchestra whose players he knew individually, with capabilities he had to accommodate. His other work included teaching in local schools and giving private lessons in Malvern. In 1885 he succeeded William at the organ of St George’s.
